overview: Guinea became independent from France in 1958. This record represents the country centered on Conakry, with its own political history, linguistic creativity and living musical traditions.

periods.title: Independence and Touré’s rule
periods.summary: Sékou Touré’s independence leadership was followed by a repressive one-party state.

periods.title: Authoritarian rule and transition
periods.summary: Touré’s death was followed by further authoritarian government; an electoral transition concluded in 2010.

periods.title: Elections and renewed military intervention
periods.summary: A 2021 coup interrupted civilian government; another presidential election took place in December 2025.

sections.title: Sovereignty and the people who live with it

items.text: Guinea’s National Assembly proclaimed independence on 2 October 1958. The country is sometimes called Guinea-Conakry to distinguish it from Guinea-Bissau and Equatorial Guinea. Its modern republic should not be confused with the much wider historical geographical expression Guinea.

Sékou Touré helped lead the break with French rule, then governed until 1984 through a one-party dictatorship. His government persecuted real and suspected opponents. Independence and freedom from repression are different historical questions, both important to families living under a new state.

Guinea completed a presidential election process in 2010, experienced another military coup in September 2021 and held a presidential election in December 2025. In January 2026, the African Union lifted its suspension. These changes concern government; the country and its people continued throughout.

Here is an attested original-script sample: “ߒߞߏ”, N’Ko, meaning “I say”. Written from right to left, it names a script used for Manding languages, including by Maninka speakers in Guinea. A short name can carry a powerful declaration that one’s language belongs on the page.

Solomana Kanté devised N’Ko in 1949, before Guinea’s independence. Its letters and added marks represent vowels and tones as well as consonants. This is a modern African invention with a continuing literary life, rather than an undeciphered ancient alphabet.

At Niagassola, the Dökala family safeguards the Sosso-Bala, a sacred balafon associated with Manding epic history. It has twenty wooden slats with gourds beneath. Its guardians preserve an instrument and a responsibility passed between generations.

The Balatigui, the family patriarch and instrument’s guardian, also teaches children balafon from around age seven. UNESCO notes that migration away from villages can reduce the number of pupils. Keeping a musical tradition alive requires future players, not just a safe storage room.

Baga D’mba headdresses express an ideal of motherhood and community well-being. A historical wooden example in the Met is almost 1.2 meters tall and was worn with raffia and cloth. This inherited performance art turns sculpture into something that moves among people.

Guinean health workers and participants helped test an Ebola vaccine during the 2015 epidemic. WHO, Guinea’s health ministry and international partners organized the research. The country contributed knowledge that could help future outbreaks elsewhere, while coping with devastating losses at home.

The study used rings of people connected to a diagnosed patient, including contacts of contacts. Researchers compared vaccination timing and tracked later illness. The 2016 final report found strong protection in that trial, a carefully measured result rather than a promise that every vaccine always prevents every case.

Danéné primary school in N’zérékoré had a broken borehole and badly deteriorated toilets. In 2021, UNICEF restored the water source and a four-cubicle latrine block. For a school of more than a thousand pupils, working facilities were an urgent part of keeping lessons going.

Parents’ association president Gabriel Sagno welcomed the repairs but asked for help with the remaining latrines. His account shows parents taking part in school life and evaluating what still needed work. A ribbon-cutting ceremony does not do the cleaning or fix every toilet.

ending.text: Guinea remains a country. The African Union’s January 2026 decision to restore its participation followed a new election; questions of accountable government remain part of an ongoing history.
